INTRODUCTIONM
In this lesson, you will learn about Pulse Width Modulation and Amplification.
Pulse Width Modulators are used to control the speed of DC motors.
Signal amplification (motor driver) is required to provide sufficient current to drive a motor.
A Pulse Width Modulator (or PWM) controls the speed of a motor by turning the motor ON and OFF very quickly.
Amplitude of the pulses is fixed; only the width changes...
The output of the PWM does not have sufficient current carrying capabilities to drive a motor. A PWM amplifier (driver) is added to increase and stabilize the output current.

PULSE WIDTH MODULATION
DISCUSSION
Pulse Width Modulators are a type of Variable Frequency Drive (VFD).
VFDs are motor controllers that vary the speed of the motors by adjusting the frequency of the input signal to a motor or control actuator.
The Variable Voltage Inverter (VVI), Current Source Inverter (CSI), Pulse Width Modulator (PWM), and the flux vector PWM drives are the common VFD designs.
The VVI receives an AC input and outputs a variable-voltage DC to the power amplifier. The power amplifier outputs a variable frequency, variable voltage AC.
The CSI is similar to the VVI except the CSI output uses current rather than voltage for the establishment of the output signal.

VVI and CSI designs have major disadvantages that limit their ability to control devices. These disadvantages include the reflection of harmonics back to the power source, cogging (jerking motor operation) at low speeds, and poor power factors.....
PWM is the leading VFD design because of its dependability, cost, availability, and ability to offer operation to zero speed.

Pulse width modulation (PWM) is the method by which a fixed frequency and fixed amplitude pulse train is varied in duty cycle by an analog signal. This method is sometimes called pulse duration modulation (PDM)...
The inputs to a PWM include a clock pulse and a DC level which are used to generate the varying width pulsed output.
The input clock pulses (triggers) determine the period (or time) between the output pulses.
The DC level determines the width of the pulses............
The positive pulse width (PW) affects the duty cycle. The PW is the on-time (T ) of the signal.
The time between two clock pulses is the pulse repetition time (PRT)...
A duty cycle is the amount of time the circuit is operational during each cycle of the signal. In other words, it is the ratio between T and the PRT.
To find the duty cycle, first measure the PRT. Second, measure the pulse width. Then divide the pulse width by the PRT and multiply by 100. The result is given as a percentage of PW to PRT.
When there is no on-time, the PW is 0 and therefore a duty cycle of 0%...
During a 0% duty cycle, there is no input to the motor and the motor will not rotate...

A point can be reached where the positive pulse width has increased in time and the circuit is on continuously. When the circuit is ON continuously it has a duty cycle of 100% and is known as circuit saturation...
During saturation, the output will not change with an increase in input voltage and nor will the motor speed increase.
Using a 100 mS PRT and a PW of 25 mS, the duty cycle is 25%.

Any PWM circuit will alter the duty cycle of a repetitive waveform in proportion to an analog signal. IC circuits are generally used to perform this function.
The PWM uses two timing circuits. The first is an Astable multivibrator. It is a free-running oscillator and generates the clock (trigger) signal.
The second timing circuit is a monostable (one-shot) multivibrator and generates the PWM signal.
To show the basic operation of a PWM circuit, IC1 is an astable multivibrator and IC2 is a monostable multivibrator.

The internal equivalents of the 555 are shown to help visualize circuit action.
The IC1 astable multivibrator is modified with D1 to generate a short duration negative pulse at the CLOCK output by reducing T time to the R x C values of the circuit.
This short duration T pulse for IC1 is sent to the TRIG input of IC2 to force the PWM output HIGH on each (-) edge of the clock (trigger).
The upper comparator causes the PWM output to go low and await another trigger pulse at pin 2 from the IC1 astable multivibrator.
The values of R , R , C , R , and C must be selected such that duty cycle is approximately 50% for the condition of no modulation input.

With a modulation input to IC2, the C capacitor must now charge to a voltage equal to ANALOG INPUT at the initiation of a monostable multivibrator action (time T )...
As the analog input increases or decreases, the time required to charge C increases or decreases, effectively altering the transition time of the IC2 monostable multivibrator.

For proper pulse width modulation of IC2, the ANALOG INPUT should range from about 1/3 Vcc to 2/3 Vcc and may be scaled using proper voltage division, bias, and/or amplification prior to input at IC2 pin 5...
The timing of the circuits is where the PWM output goes high on the (-) edge of the CLOCK signal and returns LOW at the instant CT2 charges to ANALOG INPUT (or 2/3 Vcc without an analog input)...

Now let's look at the PWM amplifier (driver)...............
The output of a pulse width modulator does not meet the current carrying needs of motors.
An amplifier/driver circuit is added to the output of the motor control PWM to increase the available current to drive a motor.
When a motor needs to rotate in both directions, forward and reverse, a full-H (or bridge) driver is required.
One type of PWM amplifier is an IC driver such as a dual or quadruple high-current half-H driver.
Inputs into a pair of internal (half-H) drivers form a full-H reversible drive sufficient for motor applications.
IC drivers often use two separate supply voltages to deliver more current to the output. V 1 is used to power the internal logic circuits..
V 2 is used for the output circuits to the motor..
The direction of rotation is set by a high input to one of the control inputs (1A or 2A).
Driver 1 (control input 1) is the counter-clockwise control input.
Driver 2 (control input 2) is the clockwise control input.
The driver pair (driver 1 and driver 2) is enabled with a high input to the (1,2 EN) input.
The power to the motor is found on the driver pair output pins.
The driver is energized when the PWM signal goes high, which enables V+ power to the output pins. This allows the motor to revolve in the direction established by the control inputs.

A low level positive DC signal produces short pulses, which rotates the motor slowly.
A high level positive DC signal produces wide pulses, which rotates the motor very quickly.

If the DC signal is sufficiently large, the end of one pulse combines with the next pulse and produces a constant DC signal output (100% duty cycle). When this occurs, motor rotates at maximum speed...
